title: Referrals and repeat work from existing clients for Painting
audience: Painting contractors in any Titan Academy business who want repeat bookings and referrals from clients they have already served.
learningOutcomes: Plan a review or referral request that is made after the client confirms the finish, and that the client can decline easily.
Write a next-service offer for painting work with a date, a scope and a price approach, and schedule the check-in that follows it.
Write referral reward terms, including the payment condition, before any referral is made.

instruction.heading: Ask at the moment the client is most satisfied
instruction.body: The best time to ask for a review or referral is after the client has confirmed the finish is right, usually at the final walk-through or when the invoice is paid. Ask in one sentence, name the step you would like, such as a review or the name of one person who might need painting, and make it easy to decline. Timing matters. In one Baylor Keller Center experiment, a late reminder brought in more reviews than an immediate one: 1.32 per cent of customers left a review with no reminder, against 2.16 per cent with a late reminder. That is one experiment only. Sending a review link or QR code is allowed, and Google provides one. Do not write reviews for clients or invent them. Do not screen out unhappy clients so that complaints stay hidden. Podium, a review-software vendor, says Google treats asking only happy customers as a violation, and that position was not checked against Google's own policy. The ACCC says incentives must be disclosed and must not depend on what the review says. Google bans discounts or goods in exchange for reviews, including for changing or removing negative reviews.

instruction.heading: Offer the next service before the client leaves
instruction.body: Repeat work is a dependable source of growth for a painter. At the final walk-through, propose the next step with a date: a touch-up visit after a set period, an exterior repaint before the wet season, a refresh of a rental between tenancies, or a common-area repaint for a strata building. Put the proposed scope, the interval and the price approach in writing, and confirm the client agrees before you change their schedule. A written next step turns a passing comment into a booked job. If the written offer goes by email or text, check the electronic message rules first. ACMA's guidance indicates that inferred consent is narrow and does not cover a message sent just after a purchase.

instruction.heading: Check in at the interval that suits the work
instruction.body: Schedule a check-in after a period that suits the work. For an interior repaint, about ninety days is a suggested starting point to test, not a benchmark. For an exterior repaint, the check may follow the next seasonal inspection. The check asks whether the finish still holds, whether anything has changed, and whether there is other work to quote. Keep it short, record the reply and close the loop. A check-in that only asks about the result may not be commercial, but a message that promotes any service can be, even when it is framed as a reminder (Clayton Utz, ACMA enforcement, 9 November 2023). ACMA's summary does not say whether one-to-one messages are covered, so check that point before you send.

instruction.heading: Re-contact previous clients before their busy periods
instruction.body: Painting follows the calendar. Spring repaints, pre-sale refreshes, end-of-lease repaints for rental properties and pre-summer exterior work all have busy periods. Plan a short message a few weeks before each one. Offer the slots you can deliver, on written terms, with a clear way to opt out. Do not use the message to pressure anyone, and do not contact a client who has asked not to hear from you. ACMA's guidance says an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days, so record each opt-out as soon as you receive it and stop sending to that client. At the end of each period, review the response and note which timing worked.

instruction.heading: Set referral rewards in writing before anyone refers
instruction.body: A referral reward works best when the client knows the terms before they refer someone. Decide what you will offer, such as a credit on the next job or a small thank-you, and write down the payment condition, which is normally that the referred person has completed a paid job. Give the referrer a copy of the terms. A study of referral programmes found that stating the referrer's reward in the invitation increased referrals across seven studies, so say what the reward is in the invitation (Xu, Yu and Tu, Journal of Marketing Research, 2023; no figures used here). Get the referred person's consent before any referral message is sent. An older Clayton Utz article (2017) makes the same point about consent. Check any cash-based reward, and its tax or contract effect, with an adviser. No business.gov.au or ACCC guidance on referral rewards was found, so those points remain unconfirmed.

procedure: After each job is signed off at the final walk-through, make one review or referral request and record what was asked and the answer.
Write the next-service offer with a date, scope, interval and price approach, and confirm it with the client.
Schedule the check-in for the interval that suits the work, and send it using the electronic message rules.
Plan a re-contact message for each busy period in the calendar, and exclude anyone who has opted out.
Write the referral reward terms and the payment condition before the first referral is made.
When a referral books, confirm the referred job is paid before applying the reward, and record the outcome.
Review at the end of each season which requests, offers and timings produced repeat work.

workedExamples.situation: A painter finishes a repaint of a rental unit for a landlord who owns three other properties. The landlord says he will recommend the painter to a neighbour who owns two units, and suggests a credit on his next repaint.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the painter do before the neighbour books, and what should he avoid?
workedExamples.reasoning: He writes the reward terms before any referral happens: the credit on the landlord's next repaint, the condition that the neighbour completes a paid job, and when the credit is applied. He asks the landlord to pass on the neighbour's details, and he contacts the neighbour only if the neighbour agrees. He does not promise a reward he has not written down, and he does not publish the landlord's name or the property address in a review without consent for that use. If he is unsure of the tax or contract effect of the credit, he confirms it with an adviser. He books only painting work that his licence and insurance cover in the state where the work is done.

equipmentAndPpe: Client record with the final walk-through date and the review or referral request made
Next-service offer template with scope, interval and price approach
Calendar of seasonal re-contact dates for painting work
No PPE is needed for client follow-up; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Asking for a review before the client has confirmed the finish.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask at the final walk-through or after payment, when the client has confirmed the result is right.

commonErrors.error: Offering a referral reward that was never written down, so the terms are disputed later.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the reward and its payment condition before any referral is made, and give the referrer a copy.

commonErrors.error: Publishing a client's name, photos or property details without consent for that use.
commonErrors.prevention: Get consent for each thing you plan to publish, including before-and-after photos, and keep the record.

commonErrors.error: Contacting a client who asked not to hear from you, or using a re-contact message to pressure them.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep an opt-out list, honour it at once, and keep re-contact messages factual and optional.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Publishing a client's name, photo, review or property detail needs the client's consent for that use. Do not write reviews on a client's behalf or invent them. If the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to your business, client details are personal information. Whether the Act applies to a small business depends on its turnover and other factors, and that point is unconfirmed here, so check the OAIC guidance.

Review platforms and referral programmes can have their own rules on incentives. Google bans discounts or goods in exchange for reviews. The ACCC's guidance on online reviews says incentives must be disclosed and must not depend on the review's content. Check each platform's rules before offering any reward.

Check-in and re-contact messages sent by email or text can be commercial electronic messages under the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). A message that promotes any service can be commercial even when it is framed as a service reminder, and ACMA has been enforcing this area, so check each message before sending.

A referral does not extend the licence or authority of the business that accepts the work. Accept only painting work that your licence and insurance cover, in the state or territory where the work is done. Licence rules differ between states and territories, and the job value can matter. This lesson does not grant any licence.

qualityStandard: Every review or referral request is made after sign-off or payment, and includes an easy way to decline.
Every next-service offer is written, has a date and is confirmed by the client before the schedule changes.
Every referral reward has written terms and a payment condition, and is paid only when that condition is met.
documentationEvidence: Review or referral request log with the date sent and the answer.
Next-service offers with the date, scope, interval and client confirmation.
Referral reward terms with the referral record and payment outcome.
summary: Ask for reviews and referrals after the client has confirmed the finish, and make it easy to say no.
Offer the next painting job in writing, with a date, before the client leaves.
Set referral rewards and their payment conditions in writing before anyone refers.

knowledgeChecks.question: When is the best time to ask a painting client for a review or referral?
options: Before the job starts, so the client feels committed
After the client has confirmed the finish is right
Only when the client has sent you a complaint

knowledgeChecks.question: A client wants to publish a review with their name and before-and-after photos of the repaint. What do you need?
options: Nothing, because the review is positive
Your own judgement that the photos look professional
Their consent for the name and photos you plan to publish

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a referral reward look like?
options: Paid to anyone who mentions your name
Decided after the referred person books, based on how keen the referrer seems
Decided and written in advance, with the condition for payment stated

knowledgeChecks.question: When does the lesson say to propose the next step for the client?
options: At the end of each job, with a date

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Says commercial messages need the recipient's consent, must identify the sender, and must carry an unsubscribe option that works for at least 30 days and is honoured within five working days. Does not mention one-to-one messages. Read in the CP-04 research on 2026-11-09.

officialReferences.title: Online reviews for product and services (ACCC)
officialReferences.covers: Says incentives for reviews must be disclosed and must not depend on what the review says. Read in the CP-04 research on 2026-11-09.
